phase1.intro:
Decisions in Java come down to two tools: if/else, and switch.

Which one do you want to dig into first?

topics.buttonText: Why does the order of my if/else checks matter?
dialogue: `if`/`else` chains check conditions top to bottom, and [[warn:order actually matters]] — once one branch's condition is true, Java runs it and skips every branch below, even if a later condition would also technically be true.
That's why grade checks always go from highest threshold to lowest: `score >= 90` has to be checked before `score >= 80`, or a 95 would incorrectly land in the B bracket.

stickyNote.flavor: 🪜 highest threshold first, or it never gets checked
stickyNote.definition: if/else branches are checked top to bottom; the first true condition runs and skips the rest. Range checks must go from most to least specific.

topics.buttonText: How does switch work, and why does break matter?
dialogue: `switch` is the cleaner tool when you're checking one variable against several specific values instead of ranges. Each `case` is a possible match, and [[key:break is what stops execution from falling into the next case]].
[[warn:Forget a break, and Java just keeps running straight into the next case's code]] — which is almost never what you want.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚦 break is what stops the fall-through
stickyNote.definition: switch checks a variable against specific case values. Without break, execution falls through into the next case's code instead of stopping.

topics.buttonText: Can two case values share the same code?
dialogue: One clean trick you'll see in switch statements: stacking cases with no code between them, like `case 6: case 7:`, lets both values share the exact same block below.

stickyNote.definition: Writing case 6: case 7: with no code between them lets both values fall through to share the same block of code.

phase2.errorMessage:
IfElseExample.java:11: error: 'else' without 'if'
        else if (score >= 80) {
        ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Without curly braces, only the very next single statement belongs to the if]] — everything after that is just regular code that runs regardless. So `System.out.println("You're a star!")` isn't actually inside the if block here — it just happens to sit on the next line. And since the `if` block "ended" one statement early, the `else` below has nothing left to attach to. Hence: 'else' without 'if'.

[[key:The safest habit is to always use braces, even for a single statement]] — it removes any ambiguity about what's actually inside the block, and it means adding a second line later never silently breaks the structure.

mcq.question:
What happens if you forget a break inside a switch case?

A) A compile error
B) Only that case runs, nothing else
C) Execution falls through and keeps running the next case's code too
D) The switch statement is skipped entirely

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Asks the user for a temperature (int)
2. Prints:
   • "Too hot!" if temp > 35
   • "Just right" if temp between 20 and 35
   • "Too cold!" if temp < 20

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the whole "forgetting break causes fallthrough" trap you just saw was such a common source of bugs that Java eventually added a whole new switch syntax to sidestep it — switch expressions using `->` (finalized in Java 14) don't fall through at all, no break needed. The classic switch you just learned is still everywhere in real code, but it's worth knowing the newer style exists.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you go make more decisions~
